what_its_for: This supplement gives you important vitamins and minerals — including iron, folic acid, calcium, and other nutrients — that you and your baby need during pregnancy and breastfeeding. It helps prevent anemia (low iron in your blood), supports your baby's brain and spine development, and keeps both of you healthy throughout pregnancy.
how_to_take: Take one tablet or capsule by mouth as directed, usually once a day. Try to take it with a full glass of water (8 ounces). Taking it with food or a light snack can help prevent upset stomach and nausea. If it bothers your stomach at night, try taking it in the morning, or ask your doctor or pharmacist for advice. Do not crush or chew extended-release tablets — swallow them whole.
dosing: The usual dose is one tablet or capsule once daily, or as directed by your doctor or midwife. Do not take more than the recommended amount. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have low iron levels or other special needs.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight (between 59°F and 77°F / 15°C and 25°C). Keep the cap tightly closed. Keep this medication out of the reach of children — iron supplements can be very dangerous or even fatal if accidentally swallowed by a young child. Do not store in the bathroom medicine cabinet where it can get damp.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking this supplement within 2 hours of drinking milk, eating dairy products, drinking coffee or tea, or taking antacids, calcium supplements, or certain antibiotics (like tetracycline or ciprofloxacin), as these can reduce iron absorption. Avoid alcohol during pregnancy. Do not take more than the recommended dose — too much iron can be harmful.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if you experience severe stomach pain, vomiting, or bloody stools. Also call if you have bright red or tarry black stools (signs of bleeding), chest pain, difficulty breathing, severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, difficulty swallowing), or if your stools are very dark or black and you are concerned. Contact your doctor if nausea and vomiting become severe or if you cannot keep the vitamins down.
when_it_works: Folic acid and other vitamins begin working right away to support your baby's development, so it is important to start taking prenatal vitamins as early as possible — ideally before you become pregnant. Iron levels in your blood may take several weeks (usually 4 to 6 weeks) to improve if you have anemia. Continue taking your prenatal vitamins every day throughout your pregnancy and while breastfeeding, as directed by your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnant women: Start taking prenatal vitamins as early as possible, ideally at least one month before conception, to help prevent neural tube defects. Breastfeeding women: Continue taking prenatal vitamins while breastfeeding to support your baby's nutrition through breast milk. Women with anemia or iron deficiency: Your doctor may recommend a higher iron dose — follow their instructions carefully. Women with stomach or digestive conditions (such as Crohn's disease or gastric bypass surgery): Talk to your doctor, as you may need a special form of this supplement. Do not give prenatal vitamins to children.
